data.title: Brekov – a Slavic hillfort below the ancient castle above the Laborec
data.excerpt: On the castle hill above Brekov, in the valley of the Laborec, stood a Slavic hillfort of elliptical plan measuring about 70 × 40 m, which guarded the road through the valley in the 9th and 10th centuries. A rescue excavation in 1971 uncovered four sunken features of a farming and craft settlement, with small knives, arrowheads, spurs and pottery bearing potter's marks in the form of a cross.
data.metaTitle: Brekov – a Slavic hillfort above the Laborec valley
data.metaDescription: At Brekov in the valley of the Laborec, below the ancient castle, Slavic as well as Neolithic features were uncovered on the castle hill in 1971.

children.text: The village of Brekov is the gateway to the Humenné district; it lies in the valley of the river Laborec on the boundary between the Vihorlat mountains and the Ondava highlands, below the ancient castle of the same name, 7 km south-west of the district town.

In the cadastral area of the village, on the southern slope of the castle hill, Slavic features as well as prehistoric (Neolithic) ones were disturbed in 1971 during the construction of a water reservoir. In the saddle on the access road there was a contemporary, and probably also an older, Slavic settlement of a farming and craft character, dating from the 8th to the 10th century. During the rescue excavation by the Zemplín Museum in Michalovce, four sunken Slavic features with an irregular ground plan were examined, probably the lowermost parts of sunken-featured buildings. Besides numerous pottery sherds, a relatively large number of iron products were found in the features (seven small knives, three iron arrowheads, mounts from the construction of the huts, two spurs, a fire-steel and fragments of iron objects). In addition, clay spindle whorls and two glass beads were also recorded in the uncovered features.

The sherds that were rescued come from larger and smaller pot-shaped vessels made of sandy clay, mostly on the potter's wheel; their surface was decorated with simple, double and multiple wavy lines, bands of grooves, stab marks and the like. On the bases, potter's marks with the motif of a cross in various combinations (in a circle, a rectangle, a square and so on) occurred relatively often. The pottery can be dated in general terms to the end of the 9th and the beginning of the 10th century.

Among the iron objects, two small knives with a volute-shaped end to the handle are conspicuous; these were widespread in the hillfort culture over large areas from the Black Sea region through the Carpathian Basin as far as the Baltic Sea. The dating of these knives corresponds to the chronological position of the pottery (the end of the 9th century).

At the settlement at Brekov two chronological horizons can be distinguished, namely the 8th century (a spur with hooks, a knife with a volute-shaped end) and the 9th century (a spur with terminal plates and the rest of the inventory).

The Slavic hillfort (9th–10th century) guarding the road through the Laborec valley on the castle hill at Brekov had an elliptical ground plan running NE–SW and measured approximately 70 × 40 m. The finds recovered by surface collection consist of 9th-century pottery, two iron arrowheads with barbs and a socket, and a narrow leaf-shaped arrowhead with a tang.

children.text: Among the stray finds recovered from the cadastral area of the village of Brekov is an axe-shaped iron currency bar with an arched end to the blade and a massive neck.

After more systematic excavation, archaeologists will be able to determine more reliably the date and the time span of the occupation of these hillforts, and to study in greater depth the material culture of their inhabitants and the relations of these hillforts to neighbouring and more distant areas of Slavic occupation. The hillforts probably had both a refuge and a defensive character, as the finds of iron parts of armament made so far testify. The occupation of the hillforts was not merely of a temporary nature but relatively intensive, and its duration can already now be estimated at approximately one to two generations. More permanent habitation at the hillforts is also attested by the quantity of pottery material found in a relatively small area. The pottery was produced by craftsmen, mostly on a hand-turned wheel, and evidently in workshops directly at the hillfort.

Future excavation will probably also allow a better understanding of life at the hillfort, whose defenders, alongside crafts, were also engaged in keeping domestic animals and in hunting, but above all in growing cereals in the places most suitable for it within the enclosure of the hillfort itself and in its immediate vicinity. Systematic excavation may allow a deeper insight into the historical background of the origin and the demise of these Slavic hillforts, and may give an answer to the question whether the hillforts could, at least for some time, also have been a political and administrative centre. The information contained in this work reflects the state of knowledge of these hillfort forms in the period of the 1970s and 1980s, the authors relying on the finds investigated in these hillfort enclosures. For definitive conclusions, however, further excavations of the hillforts mentioned, as well as of similar features within eastern Slovakia and the adjoining areas, are needed.
